title: At-Least-One Probability for Independent Events
description: A release pipeline deploys two independent services. Each service independently has a 10% probability of introducing a regression in a given release. What is the probability that at least one service introduces a regression?
options: 19% — use the complement: P(at least one) = 1 − P(neither) = 1 − (0.9 × 0.9) = 0.19
20% — sum the individual probabilities: 10% + 10% = 20%
1% — multiply the individual probabilities: 10% × 10% = 1%
10% — the probability is the same as for a single service since the events are independent
explanation: "At least one" problems are solved with the complement rule: P(at least one regression) = 1 − P(no regression in either service). Because the services are independent, P(no regression in either) = P(no regression in A) × P(no regression in B) = 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81. So P(at least one) = 1 − 0.81 = 0.19 (19%). Option B adds the probabilities, which would be valid only if the events were mutually exclusive — they are not (both services can regress simultaneously). Option C multiplies the failure probabilities, computing P(both regress) = 0.01, not P(at least one). Option D ignores the second service entirely.
hints: "At least one" is often easier to compute via its complement: what is the probability that neither service introduces a regression?
For independent events, P(neither) = P(not A) × P(not B). Then subtract from 1.

title: Z-Score: What It Measures
description: A cloud service's daily request count follows a normal distribution with mean 40,000 and standard deviation 5,000 requests per day. On a particular day the count reaches 52,500. A data analyst computes z = 2.5. Which statement correctly interprets this?
options: The z-score of 2.5 means the day's count was 2.5 times the mean — traffic was 2.5× normal
A z-score of 2.5 automatically indicates an anomaly requiring an alert — any z above 2 signals a statistically significant deviation regardless of context
The z-score of 2.5 measures the absolute deviation from the mean: 52,500 − 40,000 = 12,500, so z = 12,500
The z-score of 2.5 means the day's count was 2.5 standard deviations above the mean, placing it at approximately the 99.4th percentile of daily request counts
explanation: A z-score standardises an observation by measuring how many standard deviations it sits above or below the mean: z = (x − μ) / σ = (52,500 − 40,000) / 5,000 = 2.5. Looking up z = 2.5 on the standard normal table gives approximately the 99.4th percentile — this day had more traffic than about 99.4% of all days. Option A confuses the z-score with a multiplicative ratio; 2.5 times the mean would be 100,000 requests, not 52,500. Option B over-generalises: whether z > 2 warrants an alert depends on the chosen significance level, the cost of false alarms, and the application context — z-scores alone do not dictate alerting thresholds. Option C gives the raw deviation (12,500 requests), not the standardised z-score; dividing by σ is what makes z-scores comparable across distributions with different scales.
hints: The analyst says the count is '2.5 standard deviations above the mean.' What unit does a z-score use, and how does that connect to a position in the normal distribution's percentile table?
z = (observation − mean) / standard deviation. Once you have z, the standard normal table maps it to the fraction of the distribution that falls below that point — what does z = 2.5 correspond to?

title: What the CLT Actually Justifies for a Z-Interval
description: A data scientist builds a 95% CI for mean order value: x̄ ± 1.96·(s/√n) with n = 400 orders drawn from a heavily right-skewed revenue distribution. Her manager asks: 'Why use 1.96 from the normal table if revenue isn't normally distributed?' She replies: 'The CLT justifies it.' Which answer best explains what the CLT actually guarantees here — and where the real remaining assumption could still break down?
options: The CLT applies to the sampling distribution of x̄ — not revenue values — regardless of skewness; it's reliable at n = 400. The real remaining assumption is independence across orders
The CLT transforms the revenue distribution itself into a normal distribution once n ≥ 30, so individual revenue values become approximately normal and the 1.96 multiplier applies directly to them
The CLT only applies when the population is symmetric; for heavily right-skewed revenue a bootstrap CI is always required regardless of sample size
The CLT guarantees normality of x̄ only when the population variance σ² is known; since s is estimated from the sample, the t-distribution must be used and the CLT justification does not apply
explanation: The CLT says the *sampling distribution of the sample mean x̄* converges to approximately normal as n grows, regardless of the shape of the underlying population. With n = 400, this approximation is strong even for a skewed revenue distribution — the manager's objection (revenue isn't normally distributed) conflates the population distribution with the sampling distribution of x̄. The 1.96 critical value comes from the sampling distribution of x̄ being approximately normal, not from individual revenue values being normal. The genuine remaining assumption that could break down is independence: if orders are clustered (e.g., all from the same promotion event) or strongly time-correlated, the effective sample size is much smaller than 400 and the CLT approximation weakens. Option B is wrong — the CLT acts on the *mean of a sample*, not on individual observations; individual revenue values stay skewed regardless of n. Option C is wrong — the CLT applies to any distribution with finite variance, including heavily skewed ones. Option D conflates the z-vs-t choice (about whether σ is known) with the CLT's validity — the CLT applies equally whether you end up using z or t; the choice between them is a separate consideration about degrees of freedom at finite n.
hints: The manager says revenue 'isn't normally distributed.' Before agreeing or disagreeing, identify exactly which distribution must be approximately normal for the 1.96 multiplier to be valid — is it the distribution of individual revenue values, or something derived from them?

Once you've named which distribution the CLT acts on, ask: what property of the 400 orders does the CLT quietly require in order to work? Think about what changes if all orders came from the same burst event rather than randomly across time.

title: Compute a 95% Confidence Interval for a Proportion
description:
Write `solve(k, n)` that returns the Wald 95% confidence interval `(lower, upper)` for a binomial proportion, rounded to 4 decimal places each. Clamp both bounds to [0.0, 1.0].

Formula: p̂ ± 1.96 × √(p̂(1−p̂)/n) where p̂ = k/n.
starter_code:
def solve(k: int, n: int) -> tuple[float, float]:
    pass
expected_code:
import math
def solve(k: int, n: int) -> tuple[float, float]:
    phat = k / n
    se = math.sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n)
    lower = max(0.0, phat - 1.96 * se)
    upper = min(1.0, phat + 1.96 * se)
    return (round(lower, 4), round(upper, 4))
solution_code:
import math
def solve(k: int, n: int) -> tuple[float, float]:
    phat = k / n
    se = math.sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n)
    lower = max(0.0, phat - 1.96 * se)
    upper = min(1.0, phat + 1.96 * se)
    return (round(lower, 4), round(upper, 4))
explanation: The Wald interval uses the normal approximation to the binomial. p̂ = k/n is the sample proportion. The standard error is √(p̂(1−p̂)/n). Multiply by z = 1.96 for 95% confidence. Clamping ensures the interval stays within valid probability bounds.
hints: p̂ = k/n, then SE = sqrt(p̂*(1-p̂)/n), and the interval is p̂ ± 1.96*SE.
Clamp both bounds to [0, 1] — the formula can produce negative lower bounds when p̂ is close to 0.

title: Type I vs Type II Error Trade-Off in A/B Testing
description: A product team runs an A/B test with α = 0.05 and power = 0.80. The test concludes with p = 0.12 — not significant. A stakeholder says: 'We cannot conclude the treatment has no effect — only that we lack evidence to reject the null.' A junior analyst disagrees: 'p = 0.12 > 0.05 so we accept the null.' Who is right?
options: The junior analyst is right — failing to reject H₀ at α = 0.05 is equivalent to accepting H₀ at 95% confidence

The stakeholder is right — failing to reject H₀ only means the data did not provide sufficient evidence against it; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, especially with power = 0.80 (20% chance of missing a true effect of the assumed size)
Both are wrong — a p-value of 0.12 is borderline significant and the test should be re-run with more data before drawing any conclusion
The stakeholder is right, but only because power = 0.80 is below the required 0.95 threshold for business decisions
explanation: Failing to reject H₀ is not the same as 'accepting' it — this is a fundamental asymmetry in hypothesis testing. The test was designed with 80% power: there was a 20% chance of missing a true effect of the assumed size. With p = 0.12, the data simply didn't cross the evidence threshold; the null is not confirmed as true. The stakeholder's statement is statistically precise. Option A confuses failing-to-reject with confirming H₀ — a classic error. Option C misframes 0.12 as borderline significant (it's not near 0.05 in a meaningful sense). Option D is wrong — there is no universal '0.95 power threshold' for business decisions.
hints: Think carefully about the difference between 'I found no evidence of X' and 'I found evidence that X is false.' Are those two statements saying the same thing?
Power tells you the probability of detecting a true effect of a given size. Failing to detect doesn't mean the effect doesn't exist.

title: Ecological Fallacy: When Aggregate Correlations Mislead
description: A researcher correlates average national income (GDP per capita) with average life expectancy across 180 countries and finds r = 0.82. A health economist concludes: 'This proves that higher personal income causes longer individual life expectancy — we should prioritise income-transfer programs for longevity.' A statistician objects that this is an ecological fallacy. What is the correct objection, and what data would be needed to support the economist's individual-level claim?
options: The objection is excessive — a correlation of 0.82 across 180 countries is so strong that the individual-level relationship must exist; ecological correlations reliably bound the individual-level effect from below
The correlation is invalid because GDP per capita is a mean and ignores within-country inequality; once adjusted for Gini coefficients the aggregate relationship disappears entirely

Ecological fallacy: country-level r = 0.82 cannot be extrapolated to individuals. High-income countries co-vary with healthcare and education, inflating the aggregate r. Individual microdata is required
The ecological correlation is valid evidence for the causal claim, but establishes only correlation, not causation — the economist's error is the causal language, not the use of aggregate data
explanation: The ecological fallacy (Robinson's paradox) is the error of inferring individual-level relationships from group-level statistics. When data is aggregated to the country level, within-country individual variation disappears and between-country variation dominates. Countries with high GDP also tend to have better healthcare systems, safer water supplies, higher education levels, and lower violence — all of these independently extend life expectancy. The observed r = 0.82 reflects this co-variation at the country level; it does not isolate the effect of personal income on an individual's lifespan. Critically, ecological correlations are typically stronger than individual-level correlations because group averaging smooths out within-group noise — Option A has the direction backwards. The individual-level claim requires longitudinal microdata on individuals with income and mortality records, analysed with controls for the confounders that vary across and within countries. Option B raises a valid secondary concern (inequality matters) but mischaracterises the fallacy — the problem exists even with perfectly measured average income. Option D correctly identifies the correlation-vs-causation issue but misses the deeper problem: even using this aggregate data as evidence of an individual-level correlation (not just causation) is the ecological fallacy.
hints: The correlation of 0.82 is measured across countries, not across individuals. When you average income and life expectancy to the country level, think about what else varies systematically between high- and low-income countries — and whether all of that co-variation gets absorbed into the aggregate correlation.

Ecological correlations are typically stronger than the equivalent individual-level correlations, not weaker — group averaging suppresses within-group noise. What level of data would you actually need to measure the relationship the economist is claiming exists?

title: Compute Bonferroni-Corrected Power
description:
Write `solve(k, effect_size, n_per_arm)` that returns the statistical power for each of `k` independent two-sample z-tests after Bonferroni correction, given `effect_size` (Cohen's d) and `n_per_arm` (sample size per group). Use `statistics.NormalDist` for all normal CDF computations.

Formula: power = P(Z > z_{α_bonf/2} - effect_size × √(n/2)) where α_bonf = 0.05/k and n = n_per_arm. Round to 4 decimal places.
starter_code:
def solve(k: int, effect_size: float, n_per_arm: int) -> float:
    pass
expected_code:
import math
from statistics import NormalDist
def solve(k: int, effect_size: float, n_per_arm: int) -> float:
    alpha_bonf = 0.05 / k
    z_crit = NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - alpha_bonf / 2)
    ncp = effect_size * math.sqrt(n_per_arm / 2)
    power = 1 - NormalDist().cdf(z_crit - ncp)
    return round(power, 4)
solution_code:
import math
from statistics import NormalDist
def solve(k: int, effect_size: float, n_per_arm: int) -> float:
    alpha_bonf = 0.05 / k
    z_crit = NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - alpha_bonf / 2)
    ncp = effect_size * math.sqrt(n_per_arm / 2)
    power = 1 - NormalDist().cdf(z_crit - ncp)
    return round(power, 4)
explanation: Bonferroni correction divides the overall α by k, raising the per-test critical value. Power = P(reject H₀ | H₁ is true) = P(Z > z_crit - ncp) where ncp = effect_size × √(n/2) is the non-centrality parameter for the two-sample z-test. As k increases, z_crit rises and power falls — the multiple-testing cost.
hints: Bonferroni raises the critical value from z_{0.025} to z_{α_bonf/2} where α_bonf = 0.05/k.
ncp = effect_size × √(n_per_arm/2) is the non-centrality parameter for a two-sample z-test.

title: Instrumental Variables: Causation Without a Randomised Experiment
description: A company wants to estimate the causal effect of customer support response time on churn. Response time is not randomly assigned — customers with complex issues get slower responses and are also more likely to churn, confounding any observational comparison. A data scientist proposes using support agent workload as an instrumental variable. Which statement correctly identifies what makes workload a valid (or invalid) instrument and what the estimate would represent?
options: Workload is valid as long as it correlates with response time — the only requirement for a valid instrument is relevance. The exclusion restriction is a theoretical assumption that holds automatically whenever the instrument is determined by the firm rather than by the customer

Valid IV requires relevance (workload correlates with response time) and exclusion restriction (workload affects churn only via response time). Threat: high-workload periods may coincide with outages, creating a direct workload→churn path that violates exclusion
Workload is valid because it is determined by staffing decisions external to the customer, which eliminates all confounding between response time and churn by design
Instrumental variable estimation is only necessary when the dataset is small — with thousands of churn records, OLS regression on response time directly recovers the causal effect
explanation: Instrumental variable (IV) estimation is used when the treatment (response time) is endogenous — correlated with unobserved confounders such as issue complexity. A valid instrument must satisfy two conditions. First, relevance: the instrument (workload) must be correlated with the treatment (response time) — high workload plausibly slows responses. Second, the exclusion restriction: workload must affect churn only through response time, with no direct path and no path through other unobserved variables. This second condition is an untestable assumption in most observational settings. When both hold, IV identifies the Local Average Treatment Effect — the causal effect of response time on churn for the subpopulation of customers whose response time actually changes with workload (the 'compliers'), which may differ from the average effect across all customers. The key threat here is that high-workload periods may coincide with service degradations, product issues, or understaffed teams that independently raise churn, violating exclusion. Option A is wrong: relevance alone is insufficient; a weak instrument that violates exclusion can produce worse bias than OLS. Option C is wrong: being 'external to the customer' does not automatically satisfy the exclusion restriction — external instruments can still affect the outcome through channels other than the treatment. Option D is wrong: observational OLS produces biased causal estimates whenever the treatment is endogenous, regardless of sample size; more data does not eliminate confounding.
hints: The core problem is that customers with complex issues both experience slower responses and are more likely to churn — making it impossible to isolate response time's effect from OLS alone. What two properties would a third variable need in order to break this confounding and let you estimate the causal effect of response time?

Check workload against each condition separately: (1) Is workload correlated with response time? (2) Does workload have any path to churn that does not run through response time? Both conditions must hold — and the second one is an assumption, not something you can verify from the data alone.
